newsitem.title: UK: Ireland calls on UK to reopen "Bloody Sunday" file.
newsitem.headline: Ireland calls on UK to reopen "Bloody Sunday" file.

text.p: Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring on Wednesday called on Britain to look again at the case of 13 Catholics shot dead by British troops in 1972 in the light of fresh information which suggested there had been a cover-up.

Spring was speaking to Britain's Channel Four news, which said it had found fresh evidence to back allegations it made earlier this month that successive British governments had obscured key facts of what became known as Bloody Sunday.
The 13 died when British paratroopers opened fire at an Irish civil rights rally in Londonderry, Northern Ireland's second city, on Sunday January 30, 1972.

An official inquiry exonerated troops, saying they had come under fire. But Catholics opposed to British rule have always dismissed the findings, saying the casualties were unarmed victims of deliberate shootings.

Britain maintained that the paratroopers were shooting at ground level, but Channel Four said it had found a soldier who insisted a British army sniper had been firing at the crowd from the top of a house. Three of the dead were found nearby.
The news channel also said several of the soldiers had changed their statements before appearing at the inquiry to make their actions look better.
"Any situation like this where new information is brought forward, where there are new facts and material...I think it does warrant investigation," Spring said.

"I think it would be incumbent on the British government and the Northern Ireland Office that steps should be taken immediately to examine the new evidence brought forward and to take whatever steps are necessary."

Earlier this month Channel Four quoted participants as saying there had been soldiers based on the city walls high above the demonstration and quoted medical experts as saying some of the victims had been shot from an angle of 45 degrees.
Bloody Sunday was a defining moment in the current era of conflict over British rule in Northern Ireland, marking the start of all-out violence in the province.
John Hume of the moderate Northern Irish Catholic SDLP party and 65 other members of parliament on Wednesday called for a re-examination of Bloody Sunday.
But a British government spokesman said there were no plans to hold another inquiry into the killings.
